title: Broderbund U-Force
subtitle: The NES touchless controller with the unfortunate slogan 'Don't Touch!' — nine infrared beams, zero playability, one magnificent failure
why_scout_cares: In 1989, Broderbund Software — a company that had never made hardware — shipped a rectangular clamshell pad with nine infrared emitter-detector pairs that tracked hand position in 3D space above the device. No contact. No glove. No wand. Just wave your hands in the air and the coprocessor translates IR beam occlusion into D-pad directions. It was the Power Glove's rival in the 1989 NES motion-control wars, priced at $69.95. It flopped catastrophically: ambient light confused the sensors, calibration drifted constantly, and 'Don't Touch!' became an ironic punchline. The internal engineering was surprisingly sophisticated — 5-bit analog resolution per sensor, predating analog thumbsticks by seven years — but every unit required individual hand-calibration by cutting resistors and soldering capacitors at the factory. It is a perfect HCI artifact: an ambitious, genuinely novel interaction model, executed with clever engineering, completely undone by the gap between laboratory conditions and living-room reality.

research.title: Broderbund U-Force
research.by: Broderbund Software, Inc. — David Capper (project lead, former Mattel Toys), Stan Axelrod / Avi Axelrod (electronics engineers from San Francisco Exploratorium), Richard Bernstein and Stuart Weiss (executive sponsors)
research.overview:
The U-Force was a touchless infrared game controller for the Nintendo Entertainment System, released in 1989 by Broderbund Software — a company known for publishing The Print Shop, Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego?, and Prince of Persia, not for manufacturing consumer electronics. The device unfolded like a laptop into two perpendicular panels, each housing arrays of infrared LEDs and photodetectors. Nine IR emitter-detector pairs created a sensing field about one cubic foot in volume above the device. When a player's hand moved through this field, it interrupted different IR beams; an onboard COP320 microcontroller translated beam occlusion patterns into directional controls and button presses via the standard NES controller protocol.

The U-Force was genuinely sophisticated for its time. In analog mode, it output 5-bit sensor readings — more precise than the NES's native 8-button digital protocol, presaging analog thumbsticks by seven years. DIP switches selected between six operational modes optimized for different game genres. A planned 'U-Force Series' of native games (using the analog data) was announced but never shipped. Accessories included a 'Power Bar' for boxing games, hand grips, and a T-bar flight yoke whose underside contained IR reflectors.

The device's failure was comprehensive. Ambient household lighting confused the IR sensors. Calibration drifted during play sessions. The lack of physical feedback made precision impossible — platformers like Super Mario Bros. were unplayable. Each unit required painstaking manual calibration at the factory: technicians cut individual resistors and soldered capacitors to tune sensor sensitivity, a process wholly unsuited for mass production. The 'Don't Touch!' advertising slogan became an ironic epitaph. IGN ranked it the 8th worst video game controller ever made. The financial loss contributed to Broderbund's decline and eventual acquisition.

deepDive.heading: Origins: A Software Company's Hardware Folly
deepDive.text: Broderbund Software was founded in 1980 by brothers Doug and Gary Carlston. By 1989, it was one of the largest educational and entertainment software publishers in the world. The U-Force was their sole foray into hardware manufacturing. The project was led by David Capper, a former Mattel Toys executive who had worked on the Intellivision. The electronics prototype was developed by Stan and Avi Axelrod from San Francisco's Exploratorium museum — an institution dedicated to hands-on science exhibits. This provenance shows in the U-Force's museum-like interactivity focus. Broderbund invested heavily, launching at the January 1989 Winter CES alongside the Power Glove. Both devices embodied the same bet: that consumers wanted to move their bodies, not just their thumbs, to play video games. Both bets failed.

deepDive.heading: The Infrared Sensing Grid
deepDive.text: The U-Force's two perpendicular panels contained nine infrared LED/photodetector pairs — at the time, more IR LEDs than any other consumer electronic device. The top and bottom panels fired beams in perpendicular orientations, creating a quartersphere-shaped detection volume about 12 inches in diameter. When a hand entered this volume, it blocked specific beams. The COP320 microcontroller (a National Semiconductor 20 MHz chip) polled the photodetectors, ran an 8-bit ADC0831 analog-to-digital converter, and computed which D-pad directions and buttons to report. In analog mode (activated by setting DIP switches 1-3 to 'down'), the device output raw 5-bit sensor readings — effectively a 3D position stream — though no commercial NES software ever used this mode.

deepDive.heading: The Calibration Nightmare
deepDive.text: Each unit required individual factory calibration. Groups of resistors were soldered in parallel onto the main PCB, and technicians used wire cutters to physically sever individual resistors to tune sensor sensitivity. Additional capacitors (50-100 pF, up to three in parallel) were soldered in as needed. As reverse-engineerer Kevin 'Kevtris' Horton documented: 'The design is pretty terrible and needed a lot of hand tweaking to make it function.' Some units had resistors re-soldered and re-cut multiple times before passing quality control. This hand-tuning process was totally incompatible with consumer electronics manufacturing at scale — every U-Force was effectively a prototype.

deepDive.heading: The 1989 Motion-Control Wars
deepDive.text: The U-Force and the Mattel Power Glove both launched in 1989 at nearly identical price points ($69.95 vs. $79.95). Both promised to replace the traditional gamepad with body-based interaction. But their approaches were diametrically opposed: the Power Glove was wearable (a fiber-optic glove with ultrasonic position tracking), while the U-Force was stationary (a desktop IR field you reached into). The Power Glove sold 1.3 million units and became a cultural icon. The U-Force sold so poorly that surviving units are rare today. Together they represent two complementary visions for how the body should interact with games — both failing, but failing in richly instructive ways.

deepDive.heading: Why It Failed: The HCI Postmortem
deepDive.text: The U-Force failed for reasons that are textbook HCI lessons. First, environmental robustness: consumer IR sensing in 1989 could not handle the variability of living rooms — sunlight through windows, incandescent bulbs, reflective surfaces, IR noise from TV remotes. Second, calibration: the device required a stable relationship between sensor and environment that was impossible to guarantee outside a lab. Third, the absence of tactile feedback meant users had no proprioceptive reference — they could not feel where the sensing field's boundaries were. Fourth, gorilla-arm fatigue: holding hands extended above the device for minutes at a time was physically uncomfortable. Fifth, the software ecosystem gap: no NES games supported analog input, so the U-Force's most interesting capability was unused. Every one of these failure modes would be re-encountered with Kinect, Leap Motion, and other touchless controllers decades later.

deepDive.heading: Legacy
deepDive.text: The U-Force is a landmark in the history of touchless consumer interfaces. It predates Microsoft Kinect by 21 years and the Nintendo Wii by 17. Its raw analog sensing capability anticipated the analog thumbstick era (N64, 1996) by seven years. It demonstrated — painfully — that novel interaction models require robust sensing, environmental tolerance, and software support to succeed. The reverse-engineered protocol documentation by Kevtris has made it a beloved artifact in the retro-computing community. Surviving units are highly sought after by collectors.
